articles.title: When is October Prime Day 2026? Amazon Just Confirmed Dates
articles.summary: Prime Big Deal Days is Amazon’s second Prime Day-level sale of 2026 for loyalty members. These are the dates and details to know, plus what to expect.
articles.body: Amazon just confirmed that Prime Big Deal Days (unofficially dubbed October Prime Day 2026) is happening from October 6 to 7. The Prime member-exclusive sale gives shoppers 48 hours to stock up on household essentials and fall and winter staples, as well as get a head start on holiday shopping before popular items sell out. In fact, early October Prime Day deals are already live. To help you plan for Prime Big Deal Days, I answered the most important questions below — I’ve been covering Amazon’s mega sales for seven years, so I know all the ins and outs, and I’ve been talking to experts for weeks about their expectations. Read on for everything you need to know and bookmark this article: I’ll share frequent updates as I learn more about October Prime Day. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. When is October Prime Day? October Prime Day 2026 is from October 6 to 7. Amazon previously hosted Prime Big Deal Days around these dates, so this timing is typical for the retailer. What time does October Prime Day start? October Prime Day starts at 12 a.m. PT on October 6 — that’s 3 a.m. ET, 2 a.m. CT and 1 a.m. MT. When does October Prime Day end? October Prime Day ends on October 7 at 11:59 p.m. PT — that’s October 8 at 2:59 a.m. ET, 1:59 a.m. CT and 12:59 a.m. MT. How long is October Prime Day? October Prime Day is 48 hours long. It’s shorter than Prime Day, which has been four days long since 2025 and typically happens in July (but took place in June in 2026). Do you need to be a Prime member to shop October Prime Day deals? Yes, only Prime members can take advantage of the deals during Prime Big Deal Days. You can sign up for a free 30-day trial Prime membership on Amazon’s website or app (learn about the three different types here). Amazon automatically charges you for your Prime membership once the free trial ends. Can you shop early October Prime Day deals? Yes, Prime members can shop early October Prime Day deals as the event approaches — some are even live right now, which I’m tracking here. The best way to stay updated about early Prime Day deals is to download the Amazon app, which can notify you about sales in real-time. What are the best deals on October Prime Day? Products across all shopping categories are on sale during Prime Big Deal Days, but you won’t know exactly what’s available until the event starts. In my experience covering October Prime Day, the best deals are very similar to those you see during Prime Day in the summer: They center around Amazon-owned technology like Echo, Fire, Blink and Ring devices, small home and kitchen appliances, beauty products, household basics and groceries. Additionally, because Prime Big Deal Days is in the fall, it unofficially kicks off the holiday shopping season, so brands discount popular gifts like gift cards and toys, as well as Advent calendars and themed decor. You’ll also be able to shop Amazon’s Lightning Deals during the event: They’re flash sales that give shoppers a short window to purchase limited quantities of specific products. I recommend browsing through Amazon’s early October Prime Day deals to get a sense of what’s going to be discounted, and looking at bestsellers from previous years. In 2025, for example, NBC Selected readers saved a lot of money on the household essentials below, plus other favorites. What is Prime Big Deal Days? Prime Big Deal Days is Amazon’s second Prime Day-level sale of the year. The first one was in October 2022, and ever since, the retailer has hosted it around the same time each year. That’s why many people refer to Prime Big Deal Days as October Prime Day. Like Prime Day, Prime Big Deal Days is exclusive to Prime members and offers some of Amazon’s lowest prices of the year across all product categories. But since the sale is in October rather than June or July, there’s an emphasis on early holiday shopping, so brands intentionally discount popular gifts like toys, gift cards, beauty sets and personal tech, as well as themed decor. What is Amazon Prime? Amazon Prime is the retailer’s loyalty membership program. You can get a free 30-day free trial, and after that, a standard membership costs $139 a year or $14.99 a month. Amazon also offers two types of discounted accounts: Prime for Young Adults, which is $7.49 a month for those 18 to 24 years old, and Prime Access, which is $3.50 for the first three months, and then $6.99 a month for those who qualify for certain government assistance programs. Benefits of a Prime membership include exclusive savings during Prime Day and Prime Big Deal Days, as well as free two-day, one-day and same-day delivery. Prime members also get a handful of streaming and entertainment perks, plus they can order groceries online through Whole Foods or Amazon Fresh and sign up for a free Grubhub+ membership. Is Prime Day twice a year? Amazon has hosted two Prime Day-level events every year since 2022: Amazon Prime Day during the summer (typically July, but it was in June this year) and Prime Big Deal Days during the fall (typically in October, often referred to by shoppers as fall or October Prime Day). The retailer is following this schedule in 2026. Why trust NBC Selected? I’m a reporter at NBC Selected who has covered Amazon since 2020. In addition to numerous sales stories, I wrote NBC Selected’s history of Amazon Prime Day and Prime membership guide, both of which I frequently update. I also regularly appear in related NBC News NOW and TODAY segments. For this article, I researched Prime Big Deal Days 2026 and reviewed information from Amazon press releases. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: Glasgow weather forecast: Rain expected today, with showers continuing into next week
articles.summary: UK News: Glasgow, September 15, 2026 – Residents of Glasgow can expect a damp and cool start to the week, with significant chances of rain throughout the day. .
articles.body: Glasgow, September 15, 2026 – Residents of Glasgow can expect a damp and cool start to the week, with significant chances of rain throughout the day. The city will experience overcast skies and a high likelihood of showers, making it a day best suited for indoor activities. Temperatures will remain mild, but the persistent moisture in the air will contribute to a generally unsettled weather pattern.Glasgow Weather TodayToday, September 15, 2026, Glasgow will see a maximum temperature of 18°C, with the mercury dipping to a low of 13°C overnight. The day is characterized by a high probability of rain, with the forecast indicating a 90% chance of precipitation. While specific rainfall amounts are not detailed, the condition is described as "Light showers," suggesting intermittent wet spells rather than continuous downpours. Humidity levels are expected to be high, reaching 92%, which will likely make the air feel heavy and damp. Wind speeds could reach up to 53.11 kph, adding a brisk element to the cool conditions. The day will begin with a sunrise at 06:42 and conclude with sunset at 19:24.Umbrellas and waterproof footwear advisedGiven the high chance of rain and the generally damp conditions, residents are strongly advised to carry umbrellas and wear waterproof footwear when venturing outdoors. The combination of light showers and high humidity means that staying dry will be a priority for comfort. While the temperatures are not extreme, the persistent moisture and wind could make it feel cooler than it is. articles.title: Research centre aims to pioneer 'responsible AI'
articles.summary: Sheffield Hallam University says its Centre of Excellence in AI and Robotics has an ethical focus.
articles.body:
A new research centre will address some of the challenges in developing AI and cement South Yorkshire's involvement in the technology, the people behind it have said.

Sheffield Hallam University's Centre of Excellence in AI and Robotics, which was launched last week, already had several projects under way focusing on ethical, inclusive and human-centred research, according to its director Prof Alessandro Di Nuovo.

Di Nuovo said the overarching message of the centre was that "technology should help humans, not replace them".

"All together, we can join our forces to make Sheffield the centre for responsible AI," he said.

The centre was officially launched by South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard on Wednesday during an event to showcase the research and intent behind the centre.

"We have a proud history of changing the world through innovation, engineering and industry," Coppard said.

"We can't afford to sit on the sidelines while decisions about the future are made elsewhere."

Discussed at the launch were the projects that were already in progress at the site.

One of them, funded by UK Research and Innovation, was developing an artificial "mind" for robots that developed in a similar way to a child's brain, attendees were told.

Another project was the £6.2m Horizon Europe-funded PRIMI project, where researchers had developed interactive, autonomous robots using technology inspired by the human brain to support the rehabilitation of stroke survivors.

Di Nuovo said: "The focus of our research here, and it's quite unique, we can involve those that are usually marginalised and help to understand how they can benefit as well."

On the subject of AI's adverse impacts, Di Nuovo said: "Every industrial revolution has created change - and change needs to be managed.

"This is a call for policymakers and regulators to try to find the right balance between nurturing and helping the innovation without stopping it, and making it safe for everybody."

He added that South Yorkshire already had an international reputation for world-leading research, and the new facility would equip the region to be "the centre for responsible AI".

articles.title: Marble Hosmer sculpture mistaken for garden ornament in Cotswolds
articles.summary: The 19th Century bust, which spent more than 70 years outside, could fetch up to £18,000 at auction.
articles.body:
A rare marble sculpture could fetch up to £18,000 at auction after it spent more than seven decades sitting outside, mistaken for a garden ornament.

The lichen-covered bust from 1854 was discovered by Thomas Jenner-Fust, director of Chorley's Auctioneers, during a routine house valuation in the Cotswolds.

What the family thought was a reconstituted stone bust turned out to be the work of pioneering 19th-Century artist and feminist figure, Harriet Goodhue Hosmer.

Jenner-Fust said it is a reminder that some of the most valuable objects are not tucked away in stately homes but hiding in plain sight, waiting to be rediscovered.

Three sisters rising through the ranks of bowls

Boats stuck as silt builds up in city docks

Jury discharged in Boris Johnson wedding plot trial

The statue will go under the hammer at Chorley's Auctioneers in Gloucester later.

Hosmer was an American neoclassical sculptor born in Massachusetts in 1830, and is widely regarded as the first professional female sculptor in the United States.

She spent much of her career in Rome, where she developed an international reputation in a field that was overwhelmingly dominated by men.

Hosmer was also openly gay during a time when same-sex relationships were widely condemned, and in some places, illegal.

"She was somebody who was exceptional - a real trailblazer and a feminist icon," Jenner-Fust said.

The bust on sale depicts Daphne, Apollo's first love in Greek mythology, and is inscribed with the Latin phrase "me fecit Roma" - translating to "Rome made me".

As Hosmer's debut sculpture, only a small handful were ever created.

Historians from the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York recognise only three verified marble versions surviving today - all on display in museums across the US.

It is unclear exactly how the sculpture came to be in the Cotswolds, but the family presume it was bought at auction by an ancestor in the mid 1900s.

Jenner-Fust said the homeowners were "quite surprised" by the discovery, who had been "blinded by familiarity" after seven decades.

"They had no idea it was marble, no idea who it was by, and no idea it was so valuable," he said.

Jenner-Fust urged others to "be extra careful" when clearing out older homes, "to make sure you don't throw anything out that could be very important".

"It's a bit like a treasure hunt. You never really know what you're going to find next, and that's the thrill of the chase," he added.

"It also gives us a bit of comfort as auctioneers that there are still things out there, waiting to be discovered."

articles.title: NHS to roll out at-home HPV cervical screenings in Wolverhampton
articles.summary: Eligible women will be able to order a free self-testing kit online through the NHS app.
articles.body:
Women in Wolverhampton who have not attended cervical screening appointments are to be offered home testing for human papillomavirus (HPV).

The NHS is rolling out the self-testing kits to increase screening numbers, with data suggesting about a third of women are not up to date with appointments.

HPV is a common virus and some high-risk types can cause changes to cells in the cervix, which can develop into cervical cancer.

Eligible women will be able to order a free self-testing kit online through the NHS app.

The kit contains a swab which is used to collect a sample at home before it is posted off for testing free of charge.

If high-risk HPV is detected, the person will be invited to book a follow-up appointment at their GP surgery or a sexual health clinic.

Cellular change linked to HPV can usually be treated before cancer develops, said Obaida Ahmed, City of Wolverhampton Council's cabinet member for health, wellbeing and community, who added: "Two women die every day from cervical cancer in England, yet it is one of the most preventable cancers."

Women aged 24 to 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years or more frequently if HPV is detected.

The HPV self-testing scheme is being introduced in phases across England, initially targeting women aged 30 to 65 who have not attended cervical screening after previous invitations.

articles.title: ‘More dangerous than drugs’: BJP’s war on beef in India’s West Bengal
articles.summary: Since Prime Minister Modi’s BJP came to power in West Bengal, beef is vanishing from menus as supplies become harder.
articles.body:
Kolkata, India – It’s 12pm on a weekday, and the lane in the city’s Tangra neighbourhood facing the sole bovine slaughterhouse in Kolkata is empty. Run by the city’s municipal corporation, the colonial-era building in the capital of the eastern Indian state of West Bengal looks like a fortress, with its giant iron gates locked from the inside.

A peek through a gap between the gates reveals schoolboys running around and playing in the vast empty campus. “Those boys scale the walls and enter the slaughterhouse ever since it got shut down in May,” says Mehmood Alam, manager of a roadside eatery opposite the facility that mostly caters to daily wage labourers, as well as taxi and autorickshaw drivers. He is still getting used to the desolation, Alam says.

“I don’t think this government will let this reopen any time soon.”

On May 13, the West Bengal government issued a notice on bovine slaughter in the state, only four days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) was declared the winner in the state legislature elections that saw the end of the 15-year rule of the Mamata Banerjee-led Trinamool Congress (TMC) party.

The document mentions strict compliance with the West Bengal Animal Slaughter Control Act, 1950, stating that cows, bulls, bullocks, calves and specified buffaloes cannot be slaughtered without a certificate declaring the animal fit for slaughter.

Such a certificate can be issued only if the animal is more than 14 years old, unfit for work or breeding, or has become permanently incapacitated because of age, injury, deformity, or an incurable disease. The notice also states that certified animals may be slaughtered only in a municipal or locally designated slaughterhouse and prohibits slaughter in open public places.

The notification was issued just as Eid approached in May, and the impact was immediate, with restaurants and markets across the city and state reporting an acute shortage of beef. But the effects have outlasted Eid. More than three months later, beef remains in short supply in a state where the meat was widely relished.

That is because the certificate that traders and suppliers need to show, establishing that a specific animal meets the conditions for slaughter, is not the only bottleneck holding up beef trade in Kolkata.

All meat suppliers also need licences authorising them to practise their trade. And the renewal of these licences has been in limbo since the dissolution of the city’s municipal corporation in June, after Firhad Hakim resigned as mayor. Kolkata’s next civic elections are scheduled for December.

Alam’s friend Mushtaq, sitting next to him, is among the affected meat traders. His licence is due for its annual renewal.

He laughs cynically and says none of the six generations before him, all natives of Kolkata who made a living by supplying beef, had to suffer this fate – not under any of the past governments.

“It [the renewal of licence] was halted because of the elections, but they’ve not said anything to us about when they will be renewed. I haven’t made a single penny for more than three months now,” says Mushtaq.

There’s a giant wok of beef bhuna cooking near the entrance of the eatery, and in a smaller one right outside it, pieces of fish rest in a bubbling curry. During “better” days, both woks would have beef cooking. “We only sell the bhuna now,” he says. “Earlier, we’d make a chaap, a stew, but for those, you need better quality beef, not the kind you have been getting in these last few months.”

Prices, however, have risen as supply has dried out. A plate of bhuna now sells for 120 rupees ($1.25), up from 100 rupees ($1.04) before the restrictions came into effect, while buying 1kg (2.2lb) in Kolkata costs anywhere between 350 and 500 rupees ($3.66-$5.22), as opposed to the 200-250 rupee range before May.

“But sales have gone down by a good 50 percent,” says Alam. That’s because he doesn’t have as much beef to sell and he cannot trust the quality as much as he used to – and because many customers are now scared of being seen eating beef in public, under a BJP government, he suggests.

He says he misses a group of young men – mostly Hindus – who would visit his establishment regularly for a plate of beef stew. “And we’ve almost entirely stopped having beef at home, too,” his voice dips further. “Maybe once a week, down from nearly five to six times before. We’re just having vegetables and cheap fish now. Maybe chicken. We can’t afford mutton.”

West Bengal has historically been among India’s major beef-consuming states. According to government data, 10.4 percent of rural households and 7.9 percent of urban homes in the state reported consuming beef or buffalo meat. In an Indian context, where the cow is held sacred by many Hindus, that’s among the highest beef consumption rates in the country – alongside the neighbouring state of Assam and Kerala in the south.

Among Muslims in West Bengal, two-thirds consume beef, according to government data. Christians, sections of Dalit communities, and some Indigenous communities in West Bengal also eat beef as part of their regular diets.

The law laying down conditions that an animal must meet before it can be slaughtered is not new, but its enforcement has become stringent only now after the BJP came to power in the state.

Officially, the Tangra slaughterhouse is not shut, either. An official, refusing to disclose his identity, opens the small green door along the campus boundary wall and cranes his neck out to see who knocked. “Come back later; the head officer isn’t in today,” he says.

Asked what he does in the office these days, he says: “We just come, spend a few hours and go home.” There is no clarity on when business might return to normal, or whether it will at all, he says.

Some, like Alfaz Laiq, a Kolkata-based businessman, say they saw this crisis coming. In April, as the state held the elections that saw the BJP come to power, Laiq shut down his dairy business in the district of Burdwan in central West Bengal. He sold his retired cows to butchers and meat suppliers at discounted rates.

“If I’d bought a cow for 100 bucks, I sold it for 30 bucks, which is far below the rate at which it would usually go for,” Laiq says. “That’s still better than dealing with the headache” of the harassment that the BJP government has subjected cattle traders to since coming into office, he adds.

Laiq fears that it is only a matter of time before beef becomes a relic of the past in West Bengal’s diet.

In the past, BJP governments have introduced or brought into force strict restrictions on beef consumption in several states. Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Haryana, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka have laws restricting cattle slaughter.

Rajasthan, Gujarat, Haryana and Uttarakhand also expressly prohibit the sale of beef or beef products. Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh prohibit the possession of beef obtained through illegal slaughter of cattle. Maharashtra prohibits slaughter of cows, bulls and bullocks and possession of their flesh, while Karnataka primarily prohibits slaughter and the sale or transport of cattle for slaughter.

But those legal restrictions have also been accompanied by vigilante justice, with so-called cow-protection gangs attacking and lynching Muslims and Dalits they accuse of either cattle trading or carrying beef. In most cases, law enforcement agencies have subsequently prosecuted survivors of attacks or families of lynching victims, rather than the attackers who carried out the murders.

“I am someone who used to have beef for breakfast but have completely stopped bringing beef,” Laiq says. “Carrying beef has become more dangerous than carrying drugs in Bengal now.”

Laiq has now moved on to buying and selling goats, farming and earning money by leasing out his farmland in the state.

In the Muslim-majority neighbourhood of Park Circus, a row of beef shop owners refuse to speak about their business except to regular customers. Owners and managers of five such shops selling beef say their businesses have incurred losses of 30-40 percent since May. “All of these shops in this row were shuttered for the first two months. We have only been able to reopen them in the last month-and-a-half,” says one of the shop managers.

“Supply has been erratic, prices have gone up, so sales haven’t been great either. And frankly, the quality of meat has changed as well. It’s not a good time at all,” says another shopkeeper.

Amid tightening regulations on cattle slaughter and declining quality of supplies, at least a dozen restaurants in Kolkata have reported discontinuing their beef dishes in the past three months.

Among them is the iconic Zam Zam Restaurant. The restaurant chain’s director, Shadman Faize, says they could not compromise on quality, so they had to remove beef dishes from their menus at all three branches in the city. “Yes, we have lost customers and are continuing to incur about 40 percent losses. We have even had to lay off staff, but it is what it is,” Faize says. “Hopefully, people will love our other dishes just as much.”

Only a stone’s throw away in the commercial district of Park Street, Olypub – an institution of the city that dates back to 1947 – has for decades been famous for its beef steak. Now, though, it no longer offers that all the time.

“We haven’t taken it off our menu; we just don’t have a regular supply of beef any more, so it’s available only when beef is available,” a member of its management, who requested anonymity, says. “There has never been a situation like this in Kolkata before.”

When Al Jazeera asked Smita Pandey, the commissioner and administrative head of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC), when the Tangra slaughterhouse would resume operations and when licence renewals for beef traders would be issued, she said: “The issue is related to the Animal Resources Development Department (ARDD).”

But Nikhil Kumar Shit, director of animal husbandry and veterinary services under the ARDD, said the KMC – under Pandey – was the authority in charge of the slaughterhouse and licences.

“I am not aware of the fact that the Tangra slaughterhouse has not been operational for a while now,” he said. “Usually, the fitness certificates are issued by the KMC and a veterinary officer working with the KMC. I am not really aware of anything beyond this.”

The uncertainty over the future of beef in West Bengal hangs over other parts of the state, too.

In the city of Baruipur, in the district of South 24 Parganas, just beyond the limits of Kolkata, the local market has been running out of beef by 11am since May. “Some days, there is no beef at all,” says Sayed Saifulla, a resident of Baruipur who works as a hairdresser at a salon in Kolkata.

Until May, he says, beef was the one meat whose price did not fluctuate much, even if the cost of fish and mutton rose. Now that has changed. Beef prices have soared, too.

“We had beef almost every day for all our lives,” he says of his family. “Now it’s come down to once or twice a week.” Even with that compromise, the family’s weekly spending on food has gone up 20 percent – from 5,000 rupees before May to 7,000 rupees. “Our earnings aren’t going up the same way, are they?” he asks, rhetorically.

In Malda, a northwestern district where more than half the population is Muslim, a resident requesting anonymity says beef is now only being sold through secret networks. “If you know someone who has a cow, you can ask them to give you some beef,” he says. “So they slaughter the cow in the dead of the night and come and deliver the beef to your doorstep.”

According to him, the fear of being caught dealing with beef is palpable in Malda. “But it’s not easy for the poor Muslim to give up on this meat,” he continues. “So now, they’re risking their safety and their lives to keep eating it.”

articles.summary: Surveillance video captures a man trespassing into a stranger's hot tub and spending over 10 minutes "intensely interacting" with a rubber duck.
articles.body: Georgia police are searching for a man who police say was "infatuated" with a rubber duck in a stranger's hot tub. The suspect is wanted for trespassing onto the homeowner's property and stealing their towels before fleeing the scene, according to the Chatham County Police Department, which said the man became "obsessed" with the rubber duck he found at the residence. "He trespassed onto their property, used their hot tub, became obsessed with their rubber duck, then stole their pool towels. It's obviously not the biggest crime we've dealt with this month, but it has a lot of ick-factor. So, we'd like to find this guy so he doesn't do this to someone else," police wrote. FLORIDA MAN WHO HAD SEXUAL ENCOUNTER WITH VACUUM CLEANER NEAR DISNEY WORLD TAKES NO CONTEST PLEA Police said that surveillance video from the home in the 9000 block of Whitefield Avenue shows the man trespassing between 2:15 a.m. and 5:30 a.m. on September 1. Video footage shows the man swimming in the pool before hopping into the hot tub, where he became "infatuated" with a rubber duck and was seen "intensely interacting" with the toy, according to police. "While in the hot tub, the man is caught on video becoming infatuated with a rubber duck. The video shows the man spending more than 10 minutes intensely interacting with the duck," police wrote. Police did not go into detail about the nature of the acts the infatuated man performed on the duck, although a grainy, black-and-white still of the security footage appears to show the suspect holding the duck near his face, though it is unclear exactly what he is doing. articles.title: For the first time, Japan has more than 100,000 centenarians
articles.summary: Japan has been gripped by a declining population for decades, but one age group is adding new members and there are more of them than ever.
articles.body: Japan has been gripped by a declining population for decades, but one age group is adding new members and there are more of them than ever. For the first time in Japan, the number of people aged 100 or older has surpassed more than 100,000 – a new record in the country known for longevity. The population of centenarians rose again – for the 56th consecutive year – to 107,677 in September, up almost 8,000 from the previous year, the Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare said Tuesday. Most are women, accounting for 88% or 94,298 of the total, the ministry added. Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno put a positive spin on the figures, telling reporters, “I am very pleased that so many people are remaining active and healthy for so long.” Japan has consistently ranked one of the world’s longest-living countries, with an average life expectancy of 84 years old in 2024, according to the World Bank. In the US, the comparable figure was 79. Scientists have attributed the country’s longevity to wholesome diets and an advanced healthcare system. Though Japan has a reputation for extreme working hours in the cities, some residents embrace the philosophy of “ikigai,” which encourages individuals to bring value and joy to life. The country is now home to some of the world’s oldest people: Fuyo Kishimoto, a 114-year-old woman in Kyoto and Hikaru Kato, a 112-year-old man from Kumamoto, according to the ministry. But the aging population is also putting increasing pressure on the world’s fourth biggest economy, raising the costs of elderly care and shrinking its work force. Despite a generation that lives longer, Japan’s population of 123 million continues to fall as birth rates hit a record low. The country has also opened doors for skilled and labor workers in recent years, though the government has recently tightened up visa requirements amid a rise in anti-foreigner sentiment.

articles.title: Nepal farmers are losing up to 90% of their maize to monkey and wild boars; getting compensation can require 12 documents for a payout capped at Rs 10,000
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Nepal farmers are reporting substantial crop losses from wildlife, with rhesus macaques, wild boars and porcupines among the animals frequently enteri.
articles.body: Nepal farmers are reporting substantial crop losses from wildlife, with rhesus macaques, wild boars and porcupines among the animals frequently entering agricultural fields. A 2026 study by the National Trust for Nature Conservation found that households surveyed across 44 local government areas lost an average of 50.3% of their maize production to wildlife, while maize losses reached up to 90% in Gandaki Province and 88% in Karnali. The government has a relief mechanism for wildlife-related crop damage, but farmers seeking assistance can be required to submit multiple documents and recommendations. Recent reporting says the process can involve 12 types of documents, while the maximum relief available for damaged grain or standing crops is Rs 10,000 (NPR), subject to the rules and assessment. Lawmakers have now called for a national plan to address rising wildlife-related crop losses.Nepal farmers’ maize losses reached 90% in GandakiThe National Trust for Nature Conservation, with technical support from Tribhuvan University’s Central Department of Zoology, surveyed 1,846 households across 44 local government areas in Nepal’s mid-hill regions for its study of problematic wildlife species. The research examined rhesus macaques, wild boars and porcupines, along with the economic effects of crop damage. It found that maize was the most widely cultivated crop and the most heavily raided among those studied. Households reported an average loss of 312 kg of maize a year, equivalent to 50.3% of their production. The study estimated the economic loss from maize at about Rs 2.5 crore among the surveyed households.The level of damage varied between provinces. The study recorded relative maize losses of up to 90% in Gandaki and 88% in Karnali. Rice losses reached 85% in Sudurpashchim, while wheat losses there reached 90%. The figures represent findings from the surveyed areas and are not a nationwide estimate that 90% of Nepal’s maize crop is being destroyed.Monkeys are the most widely reported crop raidersRhesus macaques were the most frequently reported problematic animal in the NTNC survey. Some 98% of respondents identified monkeys as a problem, followed by porcupines at 67% and wild boars at 31%. Researchers also identified barking deer as secondary crop raiders, while leopards were reported as a major cause of livestock losses.Researchers directly counted 20,395 rhesus macaques in the 44 local government areas included in the study. They estimated that at least 104,137 rhesus macaques live across Nepal’s mid-hill region. Some troops recorded during the research contained as many as 198 animals.The wildlife involved also varies by region. The parliamentary motion filed in August said crop damage from monkeys, wild boars and porcupines was particularly severe in Bagmati, Gandaki and Sudurpashchim. Farmers in Koshi have reported damage mainly from monkeys and elephants, while communities in parts of Lumbini and Madhesh have faced damage from monkeys and nilgai, also known as blue bulls.Farmers can apply for government reliefNepal has a government mechanism for providing relief for damage caused by specified wildlife species. The current relief distribution framework has been in effect since July 2023 and covers 16 wildlife species, including monkeys and blue bulls, alongside species already covered under the earlier provisions.For wildlife-damage claims, farmers may have to provide multiple documents and recommendations. Recent reporting says the process can involve 12 types of documents. The documents and recommendations can include:Application from the victim or claimantPhotographs of the damaged site or affected personDamage-assessment or site-verification report, known as a Sarjamin MuchulkaRecommendation from the local ward officeRecommendation from the relevant agriculture or veterinary officeLand registration or land-ownership certificateDisability or death certificate, where applicableHealth post or hospital recommendation, where applicableMedical bills, where applicablePost-mortem report, where applicablePolice report, where applicableRelationship certificate with a deceased victim, where applicableThe documents required depend on the type of wildlife-damage claim. Not all of the documents listed above apply to every case. For crop-damage claims, photographs, damage assessment, local recommendations and land-ownership documents are among the requirements reported by Nepalese outlets.Crop-damage relief is capped at Rs 10,000The wildlife-damage relief guidelines provide a maximum of Rs 10,000 for damaged grain, based on an assessment of the loss. For standing crops, the maximum relief is also Rs 10,000, with the payment limited to once per seasonal crop. An individual can receive crop-related relief no more than twice a year.The guidelines provide relief rather than automatic reimbursement of the full value of a crop loss. The amount paid in an individual case depends on the assessment and the conditions specified in the relief framework.Land ownership is part of the eligibility rulesThe relief guidelines state that authorities can provide relief when wildlife damages crops planted on land with proper ownership documents. Farmers cultivating land without the required ownership documentation can therefore face difficulty qualifying for crop-damage relief.The National Human Rights Commission has examined this issue and recommended changes to allow relief for crops grown on traditionally used, unregistered land in certain circumstances. A parliamentary committee study has similarly highlighted land-title requirements as an issue in the relief system.Sixteen wildlife species are coveredThe current relief framework covers 16 specified wildlife species. They include nilgai, monkeys, elephants, rhinos, tigers, bears, leopards, snow leopards, clouded leopards, wolves, wild dogs or dholes, wild boars, wild buffalo, mugger crocodiles, pythons and gaur.Farmers in Madhesh have also reported crop damage from animals and birds that are outside the specified list. Recent reporting cited deer, peacocks and parrots among species for which local residents have sought inclusion in the relief provisions.Crop damage is part of a wider wildlife conflictCrop destruction is one part of a broader human-wildlife conflict affecting communities across Nepal. Government figures cited in recent reporting recorded 14,821 cases of human-wildlife conflict in Madhesh between mid-July 2024 and mid-July 2025, during which 134 people and 457 animals died.The NTNC study also found that wildlife affected several other crops, including rice, wheat, millet, potato, mustard, oranges and cardamom. Loss proportions for these crops ranged from 18% to 52% across the study areas, although some province-specific losses were considerably higher.Lawmakers seek a national action planThe issue reached Nepal’s House of Representatives in August 2026, when lawmakers filed a motion of urgent public importance calling for a comprehensive national action plan to address increasing crop losses caused by wildlife. The motion was proposed by Nepali Congress lawmaker Narendra Kumar Kerung and backed by lawmakers from several political parties.The motion says damage caused by monkeys and wild boars is affecting agricultural production, farmer incomes, food security and rural livelihoods. It calls for a national plan with clear deadlines, adequate funding and defined responsibilities for federal, provincial and local governments.The motion also asks the government to provide Parliament with a consolidated account of previous decisions, studies, spending, programmes and results related to the issue. It proposes that progress on the national action plan be submitted to the relevant parliamentary committee every three months.A government task force is studying the problemNepal’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Environment formed a 15-member technical task force on May 18, 2026 to study human-wildlife conflict. The task force includes representatives of government agencies, conservationists and researchers. Its responsibilities include reviewing previous studies, existing policies, institutional arrangements, relief and compensation systems and earlier management efforts.The task force has been asked to recommend short-, medium- and long-term measures for preventing and managing conflict involving monkeys, wild boars, blue bulls and porcupines.Parliament is examining a national strategyThe Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee of Nepal’s Parliament has also been examining a technical report prepared by the task force. The report is titled “A Brief Technical Report on Addressing Human-Wildlife Conflict in Nepal: A National Strategy for Conflict Management, Mitigation and Coexistence.” The committee scheduled a discussion on the report on August 18, 2026.The discussion places the existing relief system alongside broader measures for conflict management and coexistence. The national strategy is being considered as wildlife-related crop damage continues to be reported across multiple provinces.Nepal has introduced wildlife-risk insuranceNepal has also introduced a wildlife-risk insurance policy covering human and property losses caused by wildlife attacks. The Nepal Insurance Authority approved the policy in July 2026, with implementation beginning from July 17.The policy has an annual premium of Rs 1,500 and covers 18 categories of wild animals. According to details reported by the insurance sector, coverage includes up to Rs 1 million for death or permanent disability, Rs 500,000 for temporary total disability, Rs 100,000 for serious-injury treatment and Rs 20,000 for minor-injury treatment.The policy also covers property damage up to Rs 500,000, livestock losses up to Rs 100,000 and agricultural crop damage up to Rs 50,000. The 18 categories covered include elephants, rhinos, tigers, bears, leopards, jackals, deer, wolves, wild dogs, wild boars, crocodiles, Indian bison, pythons, nilgai, monkeys, langurs, blackbuck and orphaned animals.The conflict is spreading across agricultural landscapesThe latest research and government discussions show that wildlife-related crop damage is occurring across several different agricultural regions rather than being concentrated around a single protected area. The NTNC study identified Bagmati, Gandaki and Sudurpashchim as areas where multiple crop-raiding species frequently occur together, while the parliamentary motion highlighted different combinations of wildlife in Koshi, Lumbini and Madhesh.For farmers, the reported losses include staple crops such as maize, rice and wheat as well as commercial crops. Nepal's response is now developing along several tracks, including the existing relief system, a technical review of wildlife-conflict management, parliamentary consideration of a national action plan and the introduction of wildlife-risk insurance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: British rock band Oasis announce 38-date tour in 2027
articles.summary: Oasis, the defining rock band of the 1990s Britpop ​era, announced a 38-date 2027 tour across Britain, Ireland, mainland Europe ‌and the United States.
articles.body: LONDON — Oasis, the defining rock band of the 1990s Britpop ​era, announced a 38-date 2027 tour across Britain, Ireland, mainland Europe ‌and the United States on Monday. To avoid a repeat of a ticketing fiasco when the band’s frontmen, the Gallagher brothers, first made a comeback in 2025, fans can register to access a ​window to buy tickets. Standard ticket prices for the new tour will be ​fixed and range between $96 and $360, promoters said. In a statement, Oasis said, “Start the ⁠celebrations”, adding they would “once again return to lift the spirits of the people.” “Come ​witness the fitness,” the statement said. “It shall be a sight to behold.” The band, whose ​hits include “Wonderwall” and “Don’t Look Back in Anger,” will start with five shows in Glasgow in May before moving to Manchester, their home city in northern England, for 11 dates at the Etihad ​Stadium. Dates in Munich, Barcelona, Amsterdam, Paris, Rome, Boston, Las Vegas and Slane Castle, Ireland, ​follow before Oasis finish with four dates in Knebworth, southern England, in September, the location of ‌two ⁠concerts in 1996, where they played to a combined 250,000 people. Oasis were the biggest guitar band of the 1990s. Their debut album “Definitely Maybe” in 1994 was an instant hit. Its follow-up “(What’s the Story) Morning Glory?” was the decade’s biggest selling record. Tension between ​Noel Gallagher, the band’s ​main songwriter, and ⁠his younger brother, lead singer Liam, led to the band’s split in 2009. News in 2024 that the brothers were reuniting led ​to a frenzy to buy tickets. Thousands of fans endured ​hours of ⁠waiting, only to find ticket prices had jumped when they reached the front of the queue. But the return to the stage in Cardiff delighted both fans and critics, who ⁠said the ​group sounded as good as it ever had. A ​documentary about the reunion tour, called “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger”, was shown at the Venice Film Festival ​earlier this month.

articles.title: Hungary to amend anti-LGBTQ law to align with EU standards
articles.summary: A new bill will remove references to banning the ‘promotion’ of homosexuality.
articles.body:
Hungary’s government has submitted a bill to parliament to amend anti-LGBTQ rules for minors that were introduced under former nationalist leader Viktor Orban.

The law, which was created as an add-on to the country’s existing child protection regulations in 2021, banned the “promotion of homosexuality” to under-18s. The same law was later used to ban Pride marches.

Activists and leaders across the European Union had criticised the law for stigmatising LGBTQ people and linking same-sex relations to paedophilia.

The bill submitted on Monday aims to remove references in the 2021 legislation banning the “promotion” or “display” of homosexuality and gender transition to minors.

It would now refer simply to material that can “seriously impair the child’s physical, intellectual, emotional or moral development”.

Conservative Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who won the election in April, ending Orban’s 16-year rule, said the rules would apply “regardless of sexual orientation” and bring the country in line with EU regulations.

“We take an uncompromisingly strict stance against media content accessible to minors that promotes sexual violence, manipulation and exploitation,” he said.

In April, the EU’s top tribunal, the European Court of Justice (ECJ), ruled that the law had violated “the very identity” of the bloc.

Following the ECJ ruling, Hungarian police authorised this year’s Pride marches, which had been banned last year under Orban’s government.

On Saturday, Magyar also said the government was considering changing a 2020 law that restricted adoption to married couples, which had effectively banned same-sex couples from adopting.

articles.title: What to watch in the US’s Delaware primary elections
articles.summary: It’s the last state primary scheduled before November’s midterm elections.
articles.body:
The last state primary election in the United States before the midterm elections in November is being held this week.

On Tuesday, voters in the US state of Delaware head to the polls.

When does voting in Delaware start? Polls open at 7am ET (12:00 GMT).

When does voting in Delaware end? Polls close at 8pm ET (0:00 GMT).

In Delaware, only registered Democrats can vote in the Democratic Primary, and only registered Republicans can vote in the Republican Primary since it is a closed primary system. Also, primary elections in the state are only held if there is more than one candidate per party running for an office. Those who run unopposed already advance to the midterm general election on November 3.

Delaware’s Democratic US senator, US representative and state attorney general are all seeking re-election. Voters will also choose nominees for the state legislature and for an open seat for state treasurer.

Although control of the US Senate and House may come down to just a handful of competitive races, the seats in Delaware are expected to remain firmly in the Democratic column.

Delaware has shifted heavily Democratic since the 1990s. Republicans have not won the governorship since 1988, a US Senate seat since 1994 or the US House seat since 2008.

Here’s what to watch in Delaware’s primary elections this year.

Who is running for the US Senate in Delaware?

In the race for US Senate, Democratic US Senator Chris Coons faces three primary opponents in his bid for a third full term. His challengers are University of Delaware history Professor Jeff Appelhans, naval architect Mary Louve, and former business executive Eric Hansen. Hansen was the Republican US Senate nominee in 2024. He is now running as a Democrat and will appear on the ballot under the name “E. No-Trump Hansen”.

Former state Senator Michael Katz and US Army Reserve Colonel John Shulli are competing for the Republican nomination.

Who is running for the US House in Delaware?

Democratic US Representative Sarah McBride, the first out transgender member of the US Congress, is unopposed in her primary as she seeks a second term as Delaware’s sole representative in the US House.

Republicans Joseph Arminio, Earl Cooper and John Whalen are competing to face her in November.

As of September 1, there were about 808,000 registered voters in Delaware, including about 331,000 registered Democrats and about 199,000 registered Republicans.

articles.title: US Supreme Court rejects Trump’s plans on postal ballots: Why it matters
articles.summary: Trump has repeatedly criticised mail-in votes and has attempted to restrict them ahead of the midterms.
articles.body:
The United States Supreme Court has rejected Donald Trump’s bid to restrict voting by mail ahead of the November midterm elections, in a setback to the US president’s efforts to change rules governing elections.

The ruling on Monday by the conservative supermajority court allows states to continue sending out mail ballots as they have done for years, dealing a blow to Trump’s plans to stop the ballots before the elections and halting possible last-minute legal actions as voting begins in some states.

Trump has repeatedly cast doubt on the security of mail-in voting, citing debunked claims of widespread election fraud associated with it. That is despite the president voting by mail himself, including during the 2024 election.

Mail ballots, in place for decades, have been found to increase voter turnout and currently account for a third of all votes cast in the US.

Here’s what we know about the legal challenge to overturn them:

Voting by post works by sending ballots to the homes of registered voters, who then mail them back before a deadline.

Eight states, several of them Democratic-leaning – California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington – as well as the District of Columbia, allow all elections to be conducted entirely by mail.

Others only allow smaller elections to be conducted by mail.

Although there are cases of forgery or repeat voting, they are rare and amount to just four in 10 million mailed votes, according to the Brookings Institution.

What has Trump said about the mail-in votes?

Trump falsely blamed his 2020 presidential election loss on mail-in voting fraud. He and his supporters also opposed changes made during the COVID pandemic to expand mail-in voting.

During the 2020 Republican National Convention, Trump called mail-in voting changes “the greatest scam in the history of politics”.

His attempt to push the SAVE America Act, which calls for sweeping voting laws, has stalled in the US Senate. The bill, passed in the House of Representatives in February, faces opposition over concerns that millions of voters will be disenfranchised.

In March 2026, Trump signed an executive order directing the US Postal Service to take control of mail voting by designing new envelopes with special barcodes that would allow the federal government to ensure ballots are only from eligible voters.

For the midterms, that move would force all states to adopt a uniform envelope style in a short time.

The order also required states to provide the US Postal Service with a list of eligible voters ahead of elections. Several government departments, including Homeland Security and US Citizenship and Immigration Services, would also have the voters’ lists.

The postal agency was additionally empowered to deny mailed ballots if they did not comply with new standards or were not associated with registered voters on the states’ lists.

Democrats and activists challenged the order in several courts, resulting in a series of back-and-forth rulings between May and August.

US District Judge Indira Talwani imposed an injunction against the rule in June on the basis that it likely violated the US Constitution. Talwani also noted in her injunction that Trump’s executive order would be impossible to apply when the midterms were already so close.

But her ruling was overturned by the conservative-majority Supreme Court in late August in a temporary judgement.

The Supreme Court had not decided at the time whether Trump’s move was constitutionally legal. Rather, it only sided with the Trump administration on procedural grounds after the administration argued that Democrats sued too soon.

In the latest and final decision, the Supreme Court refused to lift Judge Talwani’s injunction.

In a brief written order that did not go into detail, the court noted that the administration was likely to fail in its push to restrict mail-in votes ahead of the midterms.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was appointed by Trump, voted with the majority against the administration, though he indicated he could support the policy at a later stage. Two judges, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, dissented.

Critics have long warned that restricting mail-in ballots could disenfranchise some voters who typically rely on this method.

It could also disrupt the delivery of mailed votes, as some states, including Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin, have begun sending in midterm ballots.

articles.body: Four Punjab-origin men have been deported from Canada after immigration authorities found them inadmissible over links to extortion-related violence, organised crime and other serious offences.The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) said Palwinder Singh, Jasmer Singh, Sahibjot Singh and Amitoz Bajwa were deported following decisions by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB).Palwinder Singh was removed after the IRB found him inadmissible for involvement in a criminal organisation linked to extortion-related violence. The CBSA said he was linked to firearms-related activity and an extortion-related shooting.The four cases form part of a wider CBSA enforcement effort targeting foreign nationals suspected of involvement in extortion, organised crime and other criminal activity.As of September 3, the agency had issued 188 removal orders nationwide and removed 111 people. articles.title: A 19th century Yorkshire mill that once employed more than 2,000 people and later appeared in Peaky Blinders and Downton Abbey caught fire again; 12 engines battled the blaze
articles.summary: UK News: Dalton Mills in Keighley has lived several lives. Built as a Victorian textile complex, it once employed more than 2,000 people and helped drive the t.
articles.body: Dalton Mills in Keighley has lived several lives. Built as a Victorian textile complex, it once employed more than 2,000 people and helped drive the town’s industrial growth. Decades later, its empty rooms found a new audience as filming locations for productions including Peaky Blinders and Downton Abbey. Now the Grade II listed site is again at the centre of public attention after a large fire broke out on Saturday evening, 12 September 2026. Twelve fire engines were sent to the scene, nearby residents were evacuated and roads were closed while crews worked through the night. As reported by ITV News, the fire was brought under control by Sunday morning, but the latest incident has renewed concern about the future of a historic building already damaged by previous fires.From industrial powerhouse to landmarkDalton Mills was built during the height of Yorkshire’s textile industry. Keighley and surrounding towns were shaped by mills that processed wool, manufactured cloth and employed thousands of local people. The buildings were not merely workplaces. They influenced housing, transport, family life and the economic identity of entire communities. At its peak, Dalton Mills employed more than 2,000 people. Workers arrived each day to operate machinery, move raw materials and produce textiles for domestic and international markets. The complex formed part of the industrial network that made West Yorkshire one of the world’s most important manufacturing regions. The mill’s scale reflected the confidence of the Victorian era. Large brick buildings, tall windows and industrial machinery were designed for production rather than decoration. But the architecture lived on as a visual record of people and industries that once powered the region.With the decline of textile manufacturing, the building lost its original purpose. Like many former mills, it faced an uncertain future. Some spaces were repurposed for new uses while other parts remained empty and at risk of neglect. Dalton Mills would later gain a second identity as a filming location, a new life on screen. Its industrial interiors and weathered brickwork provided filmmakers with an authentic period setting without the need to build elaborate sets.The site appeared in Peaky Blinders, the television drama about a Birmingham gang operating after the First World War. The mill’s dark industrial spaces suited the show’s atmosphere and helped create the visual world of warehouses, factories and illicit businesses. It also featured in Downton Abbey, including the 2019 film, which used the former mill as the setting for an underground jazz club. The contrast was striking. A building originally created for textile production became a backdrop for fictional worlds separated by decades and social circumstances. The appearances introduced Dalton Mills to audiences far beyond Keighley. People who had never visited the town recognised the building through television and film. The site became a cultural landmark as well as a piece of industrial heritage. However, fame did not solve the building’s practical problems. A historic complex requires security, maintenance and investment, especially when it is vacant or only partly occupied.The latest fireEmergency services were called to Dalton Mills at approximately 8pm on Saturday 12 September 2026 after a large fire was reported. At one stage, 12 fire engines were at the scene. West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service worked through the nite to contain the blaze and prevent it from spreading, reports said. Because of the severity of the incident, some nearby residents were evacuated. Police closed Dalton Lane and advised people to avoid the area while crews operated. Residents in the vicinity were also told to keep doors and windows closed because of the smoke. By Sunday morning, the situation had been brought under control, although two fire engines remained at the site. The full extent of the damage and the cause of the fire were still being investigated.The response showed the scale of the challenge posed by derelict industrial buildings. Open space sizes, damaged roofs and combustible materials can compromise access for firefighters. Hidden voids in historic structures can allow fire to travel behind walls or floors. A pattern of recurring fires The fire of 2026 was just the latest blow for Dalton Mills. A devastating fire in March 2022 led to arson charges against two teenagers, followed by another outbreak in July 2025 that brought twelve fire crews rushing to the scene .Every fire further cripples restoration efforts at the historic site, and drives up costs exponentially. Heat, smoke and water continually degrade structural brickwork, rot timbers, and destroy original architectural details. And beyond the physical destruction, the repeated pattern has left nearby residents nervous and frustrated. One fire is a tragedy, repeated fires are a chronic failure to secure and safeguard the property. Now, local neighbors and heritage campaigners are demanding urgent action before the historic mill is lost for good.Why Grade II listing mattersDalton Mills is a Grade II listed building, meaning it is recognised as having special architectural or historic interest. The listing recognises the building’s importance as an example of Victorian industrial heritage. A listed status does not protect a building from fire or guarantee it will be restored. It does mean, however, that demolition and alteration are limited. Owners and authorities planning for repair or redevelopment need to take into account the building’s historic importance. Listing can also make restoration more difficult, requiring a balance to be struck between the need to meet modern safety, accessibility and commercial criteria and the preservation of original materials and features. But it also recognises that the building has value in its own right, beyond its commercial use. Dalton Mills tells the story of labour, manufacturing and community development in Keighley. Its significance lies not only in its brick walls but also in the people who worked there and the industries that shaped their lives.Calls to secure the siteAfter the latest fire, concerns about security became more urgent. The Keighley Civic Society and fire chiefs have called for action to secure the building and reduce the risk of further incidents. Securing a complex as large as Dalton Mills is not simple. Openings must be sealed, fences repaired and access points monitored. Temporary measures may prevent trespassing, but long-term protection requires a viable plan for the site. A building that remains empty for years is difficult to defend against vandalism, accidental fires and deliberate acts. Restoration costs can discourage investors, particularly when the scale of the work is uncertain. At the same time, every delay may increase the damage and make future redevelopment more expensive. Some former mills have been converted into apartments, offices, studios, restaurants or cultural spaces. Others have become museums or mixed-use developments. Dalton Mills could potentially support a new purpose, but the latest fire may limit the options available.The challenge of preserving industrial heritageAcross Britain, historic mills face similar pressures. Their large footprint and strong structures make them attractive for redevelopment but their age and condition present significant financial hurdles. Preservation is more than simply keeping a building standing. It involves deciding how the site can serve modern needs without losing the features that make it historically valuable. That may include retaining machinery, original windows, loading bays, roof structures and evidence of workers’ routines. For Dalton Mills, the industrial past remains part of its appeal. Filming companies have used the atmosphere created by the old spaces, but a sustainable future would require more than occasional production work. The building needs regular occupation, income and maintenance. The mill’s future may depend on cooperation between owners, local authorities, heritage organisations, investors and the community. Each group brings different priorities, but the immediate need is shared: prevent further deterioration and establish a clear plan.A building remembered in different waysOlder residents may remember Dalton Mills as a place of work, while younger visitors know it through television. Both connections are valid. The mill’s history includes the ordinary lives of workers as well as the fictional characters later created inside its walls. A place can carry several meanings at once. It can be a symbol of industrial hardship, a source of local pride, a valuable filming location and a dangerous derelict site. Those meanings sometimes conflict, but together they explain why the building remains important. The 2026 fire has made the risks impossible to ignore. A structure that survived industrial decline, changing technology and decades of uncertainty may not survive repeated neglect and fire without intervention. For Keighley, the question is not simply whether Dalton Mills can be restored. It is whether its history can be given a future that is practical, safe and worthy of its importance.What happens nextFire investigators will continue examining the cause of the blaze and assessing the damage. Structural engineers will have to figure out what’s safe, and heritage experts will decide what can be restored or preserved. In the short term, the focus will be to secure the site and protect area residents and emergency crews. In the longer term, the owner and authorities will need to decide whether restoration, partial redevelopment or another solution is possible. Dalton Mills has already survived one major transition, from working textile factory to cultural and filming landmark. Its next chapter will depend on whether the community can move quickly enough to protect what remains. The flames may have been brought under control, but the larger emergency continues. A historic building that once employed more than 2,000 people is now waiting for a new purpose, and every delay increases the risk that its industrial story will survive only in photographs and television scenes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Jacksonville donated 20 acres for a new university campus; the $300 million project will bring graduate programmes and semiconductor research downtown
articles.summary: US News: Jacksonville is donating more than 20 acres of land in the LaVilla neighbourhood to the University of Florida for a new downtown campus, backed by a m.
articles.body: Jacksonville is donating more than 20 acres of land in the LaVilla neighbourhood to the University of Florida for a new downtown campus, backed by a major public and private investment. The Jacksonville City Council unanimously approved the land transfer and an additional $50 million in funding, taking the city’s total contribution to $100 million. According to the University of Florida, the wider UF Jacksonville project has attracted $300 million in investment so far, including state funding and local philanthropy, with further support for the Florida Semiconductor Institute. The campus is expected to offer graduate programmes in fields including engineering, health science, business, law and architecture, while developing semiconductor research in the city.How is the $300 million campus project moving forwardThe land transfer covers approximately 20 acres in LaVilla, an area of downtown Jacksonville that will become the site of the planned university campus. After the city council’s approval on 25 June 2025, the University of Florida said it would proceed with closing on the property later that summer. The university described the decision as a major step forward for its Jacksonville plans.UF Board of Trustees chair Mori Hosseini said the decision reflected a shared vision between the university and the city. “This investment will create a world-class campus that serves Jacksonville’s workforce, fuels innovation and expands opportunity for generations to come,” Hosseini said. Jacksonville City Council president Randy White also backed the investment, saying: “This is an investment of tax dollars that will pay dividends for decades.”How much is Jacksonville investing in the UF campusThe newly approved $50 million adds to $50 million Jacksonville had already committed, the city’s total investment in UF Jacksonville to $100 million. State funding and local private philanthropy bring the total investment in the project to $300 million to date, while further funding has been secured for the Florida Semiconductor Institute.The scale of the investment reflects the city’s ambition to use the new campus as part of its economic and workforce development strategy. Jacksonville mayor Donna Deegan said: “Jacksonville is committed to being at the forefront of talent development.” She added: “As our economy grows and embraces new technology, the need for a skilled workforce is more important than ever. Our partnership with UF sends a clear signal that Jacksonville is at the forefront of innovation.”What programmes will the new UF Jacksonville campus offerThe new UF Jacksonville campus is planned around graduate-level education, with programmes in areas including business, health science, engineering, law and architecture. The University of Florida says these academic offerings will be aligned with the workforce needs of Jacksonville, linking the university’s educational expansion directly to the city’s changing economy.The campus will also include an applied research enterprise centred on the Florida Semiconductor Institute. This gives the project a research component alongside its academic role, with semiconductor technology identified as a key area of focus. The university said the initiative will contribute to its wider aim of supporting innovation and expanding opportunities in Northeast Florida.UF’s plans for the new LaVilla campusWork on the project has already begun, including site preparation, property due diligence and the selection of a development partner. Rather than waiting for new buildings to be completed, the university is launching degree programmes in an existing building in 2026, allowing the Jacksonville campus to begin its academic operations earlier.New construction is expected to follow, with UF saying it will begin design, planning and new buildings later in 2026. The development therefore combines an initial launch in existing space with longer-term plans for a purpose-built campus in LaVilla, turning the more than 20-acre site into a new base for graduate education and applied research in downtown Jacksonville.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Omar Hossino: Chief counsel and national security adviser, House Republican Policy Committee
articles.summary: For many in Washington, being sanctioned by America’s adversaries is a badge of honor. Omar Hossino, the national security lead for the House Republican Policy Committee, is viewed as the staffer who has helped members get on those blacklists. “His greatest achievement: He had me identified by the Assad dictatorship [in Syria] as an enemy…
articles.body:
For many in Washington, being sanctioned by America’s adversaries is a badge of honor. Omar Hossino, the national security lead for the House Republican Policy Committee, is viewed as the staffer who has helped members get on those blacklists.

“His greatest achievement: He had me identified by the Assad dictatorship [in Syria] as an enemy of the state,” Rep. Joe Wilson (R-S.C.) said. “That means you’re really being very effective.”

Growing up in Charleston, W.Va., as the son of Syrian immigrants, Hossino said he developed an obsession in the fourth grade with watching C-SPAN, which in turn helped forge his Republican identity. He saw firsthand how “socialism and dictatorship … destroys the human spirit,” motivating him to confront authoritarians and human rights abusers around the world.

Congress is a dream job for Hossino, who named the Caesar Syria Civilian Protection Act of 2019 as one of the bills he’s most grateful to have worked on. The legislation is viewed as helping usher in Syrian dictator Bashar Assad’s downfall, robbing the regime of funds through comprehensive sanctions and punishing it for its gross human rights abuses.

When Assad was overthrown by Syrian rebels in December 2024, Hossino found himself advocating to repeal the Caesar Act in order to give the new governing authorities a chance to access badly needed capital to stabilize the country.

“When it [Caesar] did its duty, we were able to meet our objective there, the Congress repealed the law, and illustrated that its time was over,” he said. “That shows you Congress had a major role in foreign policy.”

While Hossino’s work on the House Republican Policy Committee and the Republican Study Committee is focused on advancing a conservative foreign policy, he points out that successful legislation is built on bipartisanship, with compromise on both sides.

In April 2024, then-President Biden’s request for supplemental aid for Ukraine was receiving increased GOP pushback — coming as then-presidential nominee Donald Trump was campaigning against U.S. aid for the country. Getting key GOP members to a “yes” included making the funds for Ukraine a loan, strict oversight provisions and increased sanctions on Russia.

When asked about weathering partisan whiplash, Hossino leans on a maxim a colleague once shared with him: “The administration writes in pencil, and Congress writes in pen.”

“It’s sometimes a very painfully slow, tough process. But when things pass, there’s a certain permanence to it in shifting U.S. policy,” he said.

articles.title: UN experts say Belarus justice system used to target Lukashenko opponents
articles.summary: The experts say courts, police, security services, prosecutors, and prison authorities work together to silence critics.
articles.body:
United Nations experts have found that Belarusian state institutions have worked together to repress government critics through arrests, imprisonment, and surveillance since 2020.

In a report to be presented to the UN Human Rights Council this week, the independent experts said courts, police, security services, prosecutors, and prison authorities had worked together to silence real or perceived opponents of President Alexander Lukashenko, who has been in power since 1994.

The experts said they found “systematic” violations of international human rights obligations from arrest through to detention, conviction, and post-release supervision.

They cited arbitrary arrests, torture, denial of legal safeguards, closed trials, and the continued harassment of former detainees.

“The patterns of violations described in this paper continue to the present day,” the report said.

It added that the judiciary had played a key role by legitimising abuses and denying victims effective remedies.

According to the report, Belarus has previously rejected UN criticism of its human rights record and did not cooperate with the experts, who said requests to visit the country and engage with authorities went unanswered.

The experts said Belarus violated multiple international treaties. They reiterated earlier findings that some abuses committed since May 2020 could amount to crimes against humanity, including persecution and imprisonment.

The findings come three years after mass protests erupted following the August 2020 presidential elections, which saw Lukashenko win once again. The opposition and Western governments condemned his electoral success, calling the vote rigged.

In the crackdown on protesters, thousands of people were arrested, and rights groups continue to document political prisoners in the country.

While Lukashenko denies holding political prisoners, describing them as “bandits”, former political prisoner and Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Ales Bialiatski told the Reuters news agency last month that despite recent prisoner releases secured through United States engagement with Minsk, “the machinery of repression keeps running.”

On Tuesday, US envoy John Coale arrived in Minsk for his first talks in six months with Lukashenko to negotiate the release of political prisoners.

According to the Belarusian human rights group Viasna, more than 900 political prisoners are still being held in Belarus.

articles.title: Meta to report child abuse material directly to Indian authorities
articles.summary: The move follows a BBC investigation about paid adverts promoting child sexual abuse material on Meta’s platforms.
articles.body:
Meta says it will begin reporting child safety cases directly to Indian authorities, following a BBC Eye investigation into paid advertisements promoting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on its platforms.

The investigation, published in July, found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting such material in India.

The findings prompted the Indian government to order Meta to remove all advertisements and content promoting CSAM from its platforms.

"Protecting children on our platforms is a priority for us, and we're committed to working with the government to ensure that the perpetrators of these crimes are held responsible," a Meta spokesperson said.

"To collectively strengthen our efforts to combat this harm, Meta will now report child safety matters directly to the Cybercrime portal managed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre."

The Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre, known as I4C, operates under the country's home ministry.

Meta has not said when direct reporting will begin, precisely which cases it will cover or how the arrangement will work in practice.

Until now, Meta has said that when it becomes aware of apparent child exploitation, it reports it to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, or NCMEC, in accordance with its legal obligations.

NCMEC operates a centralised reporting system and passes relevant reports to law enforcement agencies in other countries.

Once Meta also begins reporting child safety matters directly to India's cybercrime portal, it will allow local authorities to receive information more quickly.

The change follows pressure from Indian authorities and child-rights groups over how such material was circulated and monetised on social media.

After the BBC Eye investigation, the government had ordered Meta to remove all advertisements and content promoting child sexual abuse material from Instagram.

The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights, or NCPCR, also took notice of the findings and sought an explanation and documents from Meta. It later opened a formal inquiry and summoned Meta India's managing director and country head.

India's National Human Rights Commission separately issued notices to two government ministries. Its inquiry is examining whether the platform's systems played a role in selecting, circulating, amplifying or monetising the content.

Just Rights for Children, a network of more than 250 organisations, also cited the BBC's findings in a petition before India's Supreme Court. It asked the court to direct social media companies to identify and report those promoting child sexual abuse material to Indian authorities.

Its founder Bhuwan Ribhu had told the BBC that reporting cases only through the US-based system was insufficient.
